title: Babel (Genesis 11:1–9)
hookLine: a tower to make a name for ourselves, and the scattering

cards: A new tower goes up downtown, and somebody's name goes on the top in steel letters, lit up at night. A few years later, someone else builds higher. Genesis tells its own tower story in nine verses.
After the flood, the whole earth has one language and one way of speaking. People settle on a plain in the land of Sennaar. And someone has a new idea.
Not stone: bricks, baked hard in a fire, with tar for mortar. A new technology. And with it, a plan.

teach.h: LET US MAKE OUR NAME Well-known.
teach.b: First, the plan, in the Douay-Rheims. They say: come, let us make a city and a tower, the top of which may reach to heaven, "and let us make our name well-known before we be scattered abroad into all lands."
Notice what they want. Not God's name. Their own.
And notice the fear underneath: before we be scattered. A tower to hold everyone in one place, under one name. Second, the irony.

teach.h: GOD COMES DOWN TO SEE IT.
teach.b: The tower is meant to reach heaven, but the text says God comes down to see it. However tall, it's so small that God has to come down to look. Third, the scattering.
God confuses their language so they can't understand one another, and they stop building and spread across the earth: exactly what they were afraid of.
The city is called Babel. In Hebrew it sounds like balal, to confuse or mix up, and it's also the Hebrew name for Babylon. Fourth, how the Church reads it.
Babel isn't only a punishment. The Catechism reads the spreading of the nations as part of God's plan after the flood, a world of many peoples.
And some Christian readers, Church Fathers among them, read Pentecost as Babel turned inside out. At Babel, one language breaks into many and nobody understands.
At Pentecost, the apostles speak, and people from many nations each hear them in their own language. The Church even offers the Babel story as a reading at the Vigil of Pentecost.
Not one name over everyone. Many voices, understood.

how: The Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) is one of the readings offered at the Vigil Mass of Pentecost, where the Church sets it beside the gift of tongues in Acts 2.

games.q: you're on the plain, baking bricks. everyone speaks one language. someone says: let's build a tower to heaven and make our name well-known. what happens in the story?

God confuses their language and they scatter.

games.why: God comes down, confuses their speech, and they scatter across the earth, the very thing they built the tower to avoid.

practice: Think through the coming day for a good thing nobody will trace back to you: refilling the coffee no one refills, fixing a typo in a shared document, praising someone to a third person and not to them.
Notice the small itch to be seen doing it, and let it go. If you pray, you can offer it for God's name, not yours.

wordCard.voice: Babel. The city of the tower, built to make a name. In Hebrew it sounds like the word for confusion, and it's the same name as Babylon.

orig.note: Hebrew: Babel, the name for Babylon. Genesis plays it against balal, to confuse.
